title: Codependency
description: A dysfunctional dynamic where one person enables another's poor behavior, relying on that person for their own self-worth.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Codependency is a system where one person needs the other to be dysfunctional, sick, or irresponsible so they can play the role of the 'savior' or 'caretaker'. It is the addiction to being needed, often masquerading as extreme love or self-sacrifice.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Bailing out a partner financially over and over again while they refuse to work.
Making excuses for a partner's abusive behavior to friends and family.
Feeling totally lost, anxious, or purposeless when not fixing someone else's crisis.
Neglecting your own hygiene, career, or friendships to manage someone else's life.

sections.title: Why It Happens
content: A psychological fear that if the other person becomes healthy and independent, they will leave.
Childhood conditioning where the person was forced to caretake a volatile or addicted parent.
A desire to strictly control an unpredictable situation by becoming indispensable.
Low self-esteem that dictates 'I am only valuable when I am useful'.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: The Caretaker: Endlessly managing logistics, solving crises, and absorbing the emotional weight of two people.
The Taker: Exploiting the Caretaker's lack of boundaries, remaining infantile, and outsourcing all personal responsibility.
Martyrdom: The Caretaker constantly complaining about how hard they work for the relationship, yet explicitly refusing to change the dynamic.

sections.title: Healthy Version
sections.content: Interdependence: Two independent, capable adults choosing to rely on each other for mutual support. Both parties can function alone, but choose to collaborate. There is a balance of give and take, and neither person requires the other to be 'broken'.

sections.title: Unhealthy Version
sections.content: Codependency is inherently unhealthy. The most severe version is Enmeshment, where all boundaries collapse and neither individual knows where their emotions end and their partner's begin. If one person is sad, the other feels obligated to be sad.

sections.title: Real-Life Scenarios
content: Family: A mother doing her 30-year-old son's laundry while complaining that he 'just can't survive without her'.
Marriage: A spouse calling into work 'sick' on behalf of their partner who is too hungover to do it themselves.
Friendship: A friend who only reaches out when their life is falling apart, and you drop everything to fix it, while ignoring your own deadlines.

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You feel resentment toward the person you are 'helping' but cannot stop helping them.
You feel severe panic at the thought of leaving the other person to face the natural consequences of their own actions.
Your mood is entirely dictated by whether your partner is having a 'good day' or a 'bad day'.
You constantly try to control or manage their behavior for 'their own good'.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: Mistake: Believing codependency is 'loving too much'. Reality: Codependency is highly controlling. You are stealing the other person's agency and natural consequences because dealing with their failure makes YOU uncomfortable.

sections.title: Protection Strategies
content: Practice 'Detachment with Love': Allow the person to face the consequences of their actions without bailing them out.
Stop offering unsolicited advice. Wait to be asked for help.
Build an identity completely separate from the relationship. Re-engage with old hobbies and friends.
Set strict boundaries around what behavior you will fund, support, or tolerate.

sections.title: Outcome Patterns
content: If the Caretaker stops enabling, the Taker will escalate behaviors (extinction burst) to force the Caretaker back into line.
If the dynamic continues, it ends in severe burnout, physical illness for the Caretaker, and suspended stagnation for the Taker.
If both parties agree to change, a highly painful but necessary restructure of power and responsibility must occur.

sections.title: Reality Check
sections.content: In a codependent dynamic, the 'savior' is just as sick as the 'victim'. Enabling someone's destruction is not an act of kindness; it is an act of control to soothe your own anxiety.
